Autoimmune gastritis spares the fundus but involves the antrum extensively.
correctOption: H. pylori gastritis is characterized by subepithelial plasma cells and pit abscesses.
optionExplanations: Diffuse thinning of the oxyntic mucosa is a hallmark of autoimmune atrophic gastritis; H. pylori gastritis is typically antral-predominant or patchy.
Autoimmune gastritis results in hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria (decreased acid) and subsequent G-cell hyperplasia, not atrophy, due to lack of feedback inhibition.
H. pylori gastritis is characterized by a superficial infiltrate of plasma cells and neutrophils that cross the basement membrane to form pit abscesses.
The opposite is true: H. pylori inflammation is typically superficial in the lamina propria, while autoimmune inflammation is deeper and centered on the glands.
Autoimmune gastritis typically involves the body and fundus (oxyntic mucosa) and characteristically spares the antrum.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 767 (Book Page): The inflammatory infiltrate includes large numbers of plasma cells, often in clusters or sheets, within the superficial lamina propria... Neutrophils infiltrate across the basement membrane and accumulate in the lumens of gastric glands, or pits, to create pit abscesses.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
statement: In the pathogenesis of Peptic Ulcer Disease, why does H. pylori infection limited to the gastric antrum specifically increase the risk of duodenal ulceration?
options: It stimulates the migration of chief cells to the duodenum, increasing pepsinogen levels.
It reduces the production of protective bicarbonate in the proximal duodenum via direct toxin release.
It triggers hypergastrinemia which increases parietal cell mass and acid secretion.
It causes widespread parietal cell atrophy in the body, leading to compensatory gastrin spikes.
It induces intestinal metaplasia in the antrum that secretes ectopic hydrochloric acid.
correctOption: It triggers hypergastrinemia which increases parietal cell mass and acid secretion.
optionExplanations: H. pylori does not cause the migration of chief cells; chief cells remain in the gastric oxyntic glands and secrete pepsinogen, which is converted to pepsin by the excess acid.

While duodenal bicarbonate is decreased in PUD, the primary mechanism linked to antral H. pylori is the increased acid load from the stomach rather than a direct duodenal toxin effect on bicarbonate transporters.

Antral-restricted H. pylori infection results in hypergastrinemia. Gastrin stimulates the growth and activity of parietal cells in the body/fundus, leading to hyperchlorhydria, which overwhelms duodenal mucosal defenses.
Parietal cell atrophy occurs in pangastritis or autoimmune gastritis, which actually reduces acid secretion and protects against duodenal ulcers.
Intestinal metaplasia involves the replacement of gastric mucosa with goblet-cell-containing intestinal epithelium; it does not secrete acid.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 767 (Book Page): When inflammation remains limited to the antrum, modestly increased local gastrin production can augment parietal cell mass within the gastric body and increase acid secretion that leads to greater risk of gastric or duodenal peptic ulcer disease.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
coreConcept: Morphological contrast between Stress and Peptic Ulcers
statement: When distinguishing between acute stress ulcers and chronic peptic ulcers during a post-mortem or endoscopic examination, which feature is most characteristic of stress-related lesions?
options: The adjacent mucosa typically shows extensive chronic gastritis
They are often multiple and can be found anywhere in the stomach
They always penetrate the full thickness of the muscularis propria
They are associated with prominent scarring and blood vessel thickening
They are typically solitary and located in the antrum
correctOption: They are often multiple and can be found anywhere in the stomach
optionExplanations: Stress ulcers typically arise in relatively normal adjacent mucosa, unlike peptic ulcers which usually develop on a background of chronic H. pylori gastritis.
Stress ulcers are characterized by their multiplicity and wide distribution throughout the gastric surface, distinguishing them from the focal nature of peptic disease.
While stress ulcers can penetrate the mucosa, they are often shallow erosions; chronic peptic ulcers are more likely to have deep penetration limited by muscularis or adjacent organs.
Scarring and vessel thickening are hallmarks of chronic peptic ulcers; stress ulcers lack these features as they are acute and heal without significant fibrosis.
Chronic peptic ulcers are typically solitary and predilect for the antrum or proximal duodenum, whereas stress ulcers are often numerous.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 766 (Book Page): Unlike peptic ulcers, which are usually solitary and located in the antrum, acute stress ulcers are found anywhere in the stomach and are often multiple.

category: Describe the salient features (etiology, pathogenesis and morphology) of peptic ulcer disease
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with multiple chronic ulcers in the stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum. Laboratory evaluation reveals a massive overproduction of gastric acid. Which underlying condition is most likely responsible for this presentation?
options: Chronic NSAID-induced gastropathy
Autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis
Infection with CagA-positive H. pylori
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Systemic sclerosis associated GAVE
correctOption: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
optionExplanations: NSAIDs typically cause gastric or proximal duodenal ulcers, but multiple ulcers extending into the jejunum are highly classic for a hypergastrinemic state.
Autoimmune gastritis causes achlorhydria (lack of acid) due to parietal cell loss, which actually protects against duodenal and jejunal ulcers.
H. pylori generally causes ulcers in the antrum or proximal duodenum; jejunal ulcers are not a standard feature of H. pylori infection.

Correct. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome involves a gastrin-secreting tumor that causes extreme gastric acid hypersecretion, resulting in multiple, often refractory ulcers throughout the upper GI tract, including the jejunum.
GAVE (Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia) causes bleeding from ectatic vessels in the antrum (watermelon stomach) but does not typically cause deep peptic ulceration in the jejunum.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 767 (Book Page): Table 17.3 Risk Factors for Peptic Ulcer Disease... Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (PUD of stomach, duodenum, and jejunum).

category: Pylori in causing peptic ulcer disease
statement: Histopathological examination of a gastric biopsy shows characteristic 'corkscrew profiles' and foveolar cell hyperplasia. In which of the following conditions are these specific reactive epithelial changes most prominently observed?
options: Gastritis cystica profunda
Ménétrier disease with protein loss
Gastropathy and mild acute gastritis
Early-stage gastric adenocarcinoma
Autoimmune atrophic gastritis
correctOption: Gastropathy and mild acute gastritis
optionExplanations: Gastritis cystica profunda involves the entrapment of epithelial-lined cysts in deeper layers, rather than being defined by surface corkscrew profiles.
Ménétrier disease involves giant cerebriform enlargement and diffuse hyperplasia, but the 'corkscrew profile' terminology is specifically used for reactive gastropathy.
Correct. Corkscrew-shaped foveolar hyperplasia is a classic histological hallmark of reactive gastropathy or mild acute gastritis.
Adenocarcinoma is characterized by atypia and invasion, whereas corkscrew profiles represent a reactive, non-neoplastic proliferation.
Autoimmune gastritis is characterized by atrophy of the glands and intestinal metaplasia, not the specific corkscrew foveolar hyperplasia associated with irritants.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 766 (Book Page): foveolar cell hyperplasia, with characteristic corkscrew profiles and epithelial proliferation, is often present [in gastropathy and mild acute gastritis].

category: Discuss the role of H
coreConcept: Acid Secretion, Atrophy, and Malignancy Risk
statement: A 55-year-old male from a rural area presents with chronic epigastric discomfort. Biopsy reveals patchy atrophy and intestinal metaplasia in the gastric body and fundus, along with a dense lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate. His gastric acid secretion is significantly reduced. Which of the following best describes his future risk profile regarding gastrointestinal pathology?
options: High risk for duodenal ulcers but low risk for gastric adenocarcinoma.
Low risk for both gastric adenocarcinoma and MALToma.
Low risk for duodenal ulcers but high risk for gastric adenocarcinoma.
High risk for both duodenal ulcers and gastric lymphoma.
High risk for gastroesophageal reflux disease due to hyperchlorhydria.
correctOption: Low risk for duodenal ulcers but high risk for gastric adenocarcinoma.
optionExplanations: Reduced acid secretion due to body atrophy (loss of parietal cells) actually decreases the risk of duodenal ulcers.
This patient is at high risk for both gastric adenocarcinoma (due to metaplasia) and lymphoma (due to chronic H. pylori-induced lymphoid aggregates).
The loss of parietal cells (atrophy) reduces acid production, protecting against duodenal ulcers, but the resulting intestinal metaplasia significantly increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.
While he is at risk for MALToma (lymphoma), his duodenal ulcer risk is low because of the decreased parietal cell mass/acid secretion.
The patient has reduced acid secretion (hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria), not hyperchlorhydria, making reflux-related injury less likely to be driven by acid.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 767 (Book Page): Decreased acid secretion in H. pylori gastritis with atrophy reduces the risk of gastric and duodenal ulcers. This results in an inverse relationship between gastric adenocarcinoma, which is associated with atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, and duodenal ulcers, which are associated with increased acid secretion.

category: Pylori in causing peptic ulcer disease
coreConcept: MALToma Risk in H. pylori Gastritis
statement: A pathologist examining a gastric biopsy from a patient with chronic H. pylori infection identifies clusters of plasma cells in the superficial lamina propria and lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers. What is the most significant clinical risk associated with these specific lymphoid aggregates?
options: They have the potential to transform into lymphoma.
They represent the site of primary vitamin B12 absorption interference.
They indicate a high likelihood of concurrent Crohn's disease.
They act as a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus.
They are a diagnostic hallmark of acute stress-induced gastropathy.
correctOption: They have the potential to transform into lymphoma.
optionExplanations: The induced Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT) is a characteristic response to chronic H. pylori and can undergo malignant transformation into MALT lymphoma.
Vitamin B12 interference is a feature of autoimmune gastritis where parietal cells (and intrinsic factor) are lost, not primarily a function of H. pylori lymphoid aggregates.
While Crohn's can involve the stomach, H. pylori-induced MALT is a distinct pathological entity not associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
Lymphoid aggregates in the stomach are related to MALT and gastric risks, not esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
Stress-induced gastropathy is characterized by ischemia and acute erosions, typically lacking the chronic organized lymphoid structures seen in H. pylori infection.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 767 (Book Page): Lymphoid aggregates, some with germinal centers, are frequently present (Fig. 17.13C) and represent induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) that has the potential to transform into lymphoma.

category: Describe salient features of acute & chronic gastritis
statement: A patient with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) develops significant gastric mucosal injury. Which specific biochemical mechanism is responsible for the impaired mucosal defense in this uremic environment?
options: Ischemic injury mediated by systemic hypotension
Reduced epithelial restitution due to increased urea levels
Inhibition of gastric bicarbonate transporters by ammonium ions
Direct inhibition of COX-1 dependent prostaglandin synthesis
Stimulation of vagal nuclei leading to acid hypersecretion
correctOption: Inhibition of gastric bicarbonate transporters by ammonium ions
optionExplanations: Ischemic injury due to splanchnic vasoconstriction or systemic hypotension is the hallmark of stress-related mucosal disease (shock/sepsis), not the specific biochemical pathway of uremia.
While epithelial renewal can be affected by various agents (like chemotherapy), the text specifically identifies the inhibition of bicarbonate transporters as the key defect in uremia.
In uremia, high levels of urea are converted to ammonium ions, which specifically inhibit the bicarbonate transporters in the gastric mucosa, neutralizing the protective neutral pH layer.
Inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 is the primary mechanism for NSAID-induced gastritis, not uremic-related injury.
Vagal nuclei stimulation leading to hypersecretion is the mechanism for Cushing ulcers (associated with intracranial injury), not uremic gastropathy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 765 (Book Page): Inhibition of gastric bicarbonate transporters by ammonium ions can result in gastric injury in uremic patients and those infected with urease-secreting H. pylori.

category: Pylori in causing peptic ulcer disease
statement: In a demographic study of gastric pathology, it is noted that certain populations have a significantly higher prevalence of gastric cancer. Which bacterial genotype is most likely present in 90% of H. pylori isolates from these high-risk populations?
options: Flagella-deficient strains
CagA-positive strains
CagA-negative strains
Urease-negative strains
Adhesin-deficient strains
correctOption: CagA-positive strains
optionExplanations: Flagella are required for initial colonization; strains lacking them would be unable to reach the epithelium and thus would not be prevalent in any infected population.

The CagA (cytotoxin-associated gene A) product is a major virulence factor. Strains expressing CagA are better at inducing proinflammatory cytokines and atrophy, explaining their high prevalence (90%) in regions with high gastric cancer rates.
CagA-negative strains are less virulent and are associated with a lower risk of progressing to severe inflammation, atrophy, and gastric adenocarcinoma.
Urease is essential for H. pylori survival in any environment; a urease-negative strain would likely not colonize the stomach effectively at all, regardless of cancer risk.
Adhesins are necessary for persistent infection; without them, the bacteria would be cleared by gastric emptying and would not be a factor in long-term carcinogenesis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 767 (Book Page): For example, the CagA gene is present in 50% of H. pylori isolates overall but in 90% of H. pylori isolates in populations with an increased prevalence of gastric cancer.
